value: This article explores the concept of a "frozen operating system"—an OS whose core codebase never changes, aiming for "infinite maturity" and timeless stability akin to ancient infrastructure or fundamental internet protocols. It defines what constitutes such an OS, distinguishing between unchanging system software and flexible user code, and proposes design principles like "Kelvin versioning" to track progress towards a frozen state. The paper introduces a "palm-tree" dependency model, separating an exclusive, convergent "trunk" of core components that aspire to freeze from flexible, divergent "fronds" representing userspace applications. Urbit is presented as a practical example of an OS designed with these principles, demonstrating how its deeply layered architecture, particularly at its lowest levels, is approaching this "absolute zero" to create truly permanent and reliable digital infrastructure.
